opus-5.5.text:
I tend to think about it as a few nested layers, roughly ordered by timescale and abstraction.

At the very bottom you have the physical interaction layer: contact, forces, friction, compliance. This is where the robot's body actually meets the world, and it runs at very high frequency, hundreds or thousands of hertz. A lot of what makes manipulation hard lives here, because the world is messy, objects deform, slip, and you can't perfectly model any of it.

Above that is what I'd call the skill or motor control layer. These are short-horizon behaviors like grasping a mug, opening a drawer, inserting a peg. This is where much of the recent progress in robot learning has happened, with imitation learning from human demonstrations and visuomotor policies that map pixels to actions.

Then there's the task or planning layer, which is about composing those skills over longer horizons. If you want a robot to make breakfast, it needs to reason about the order of things, what preconditions need to hold, what to do when something fails midway. That's a lot of my own research interest: how you get structured, compositional reasoning on top of learned skills, and how the two layers talk to each other.

And at the top is the semantic or goal layer: understanding what a human actually wants, grounding language and intent into something the lower layers can act on. Foundation models have really changed what's possible here.

The interesting research questions, I think, are less about any single layer and more about the interfaces between them. What should the abstraction be between planning and skills? How do you propagate uncertainty or failure from the physical layer back up to the planner? Humans do this seamlessly. We don't think about finger forces when we decide to make coffee, but when the lid is stuck, we immediately adapt. Getting that kind of fluid, bidirectional flow across layers is, to me, one of the central challenges for embodied AI.

r001.rationale: The response describes layers from physical interaction through motor control, planning, and goals, but it does not clearly distinguish representing how the world should change from generating the agent’s actions.

r002.rationale: It mentions human demonstrations as data for learned motor skills, but does not state that human data is particularly suited to informing how the world should change.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I tend to think about it, there are really three layers, and they operate at very different timescales and levels of abstraction.

At the bottom you have the physical layer, which is contact and dynamics. This is the robot's hand actually touching an object, the friction, the forces, the fact that the world pushes back. It runs at hundreds of hertz, it's noisy, and it's where most of the hard failures actually happen. A grasp slipping, a cup tipping over. You can't reason your way out of those problems, you have to feel them.

Above that is what I'd call the skill layer. These are short-horizon behaviors that have some semantic meaning, like "pick up the mug" or "open the drawer." They're grounded in perception, they're closed-loop, and they last maybe a few seconds. This is where a lot of the imitation learning and policy learning work lives, because it's a sweet spot where you can collect demonstrations and the behavior is still fairly local.

Then on top you have the task layer, which is about sequencing and reasoning. If I want to make coffee, what has to happen in what order, what are the preconditions, what do I do if the mug isn't where I expected. This is the layer where language models have suddenly become very useful, because it looks a lot like planning over symbols.

The reason I find this decomposition useful rather than just tidy is that the interfaces between the layers are where the research questions are. How does a task planner know a skill is likely to fail before it tries it? How does a skill expose enough of what it's sensing so the planner can replan? Historically those were handled by hand-written abstractions, and a lot of my work has been about learning those abstractions from data instead. But I'll also say the boundaries are getting blurrier. End-to-end models are starting to span two of these layers at once, and whether we should keep the hierarchy explicit or let it emerge is one of the genuinely open debates in the field right now.

astra-6.text:
I think about it in three layers. At the lowest level, there’s the physical interaction: how you move your body, make contact with an object, and respond to what you sense. If you’re picking up a cup, that means controlling your hand and adjusting your grip as you touch it.

Then there’s the level of skills and actions: picking up the cup, opening a drawer, pouring water. Each of those involves many small movements, but you can reason about it as one meaningful action.

Above that is the task level: what are you trying to accomplish, and how do you put those skills together? If the goal is to make breakfast, you need to decide what to do, in what order, and what to change if something doesn’t work.

Those layers have to communicate. A plan might look perfectly reasonable until you try to execute it and discover that an object is too heavy or something is out of reach. So embodied intelligence involves continually connecting your goals to what your body can actually do in the world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a hierarchy. At the highest level, the agent needs to understand the goal: what am I trying to accomplish? Then there’s a planning layer that breaks that goal into steps. If I want to make coffee, I might need to find a cup, put it under the machine, and press a button.

Below that is the level of skills: how do I grasp the cup, or move it without spilling? And at the lowest level, there’s control—the continuous coordination of movement based on sensory feedback.

But these layers have to interact. If the cup isn’t where I expected, that changes my plan. So an embodied agent isn’t just taking an instruction and executing a fixed sequence. It’s constantly connecting what it wants to do with what the world is actually telling it.
